title: Ἔρις
titleEn: The Quarrel and the Drawn Sword — Iliad 1.101–205
part: The Quarrel and the Drawn Sword (1.101–205)
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Calchas sits down and Agamemnon rises in fury, accusing the seer of never prophesying anything but ill. He will give Chryseis back, he says, but only if he is given another prize at once. Achilles answers that there is no common store left to draw on, and Agamemnon threatens to take the prize of Achilles, Ajax or Odysseus, and proposes sending Chryseis home on a ship. Achilles calls him shameless and greedy, says he came to Troy for Agamemnon’s sake and not from any quarrel with the Trojans, and threatens to sail home to Phthia. Agamemnon tells him to go, says he will take Briseis from his hut to show who is stronger, and Achilles, torn between drawing his sword and mastering his anger, has the blade half out when Athena, sent by Hera, stands behind him, visible to him alone, and takes him by the hair. He knows her, and asks why she has come.

sentences.t: ἤτοι ὅ γ’ ὣς εἰπὼν κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζετο·
sentences.tr: ētoi ho g’ hōs eipōn kat’ ar’ hezeto·
sentences.l: He then, having so spoken, sat down;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and sat down;
sentences.n: ὅ γε is Calchas, who has just finished; the line is word for word 1.68, where it sat Achilles down and brought Calchas to his feet, and the English is the same. ἤτοι is printed as one word, ὣς εἰπών is ‘having so spoken’, and κατὰ … ἕζετο ‘sat down’ is a tmesis, the preverb κατά standing apart from its verb with ἄρ’ between.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δ’ ἀνέστη
ἥρως Ἀτρεΐδης εὐρὺ κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων
ἀχνύμενος·
sentences.tr:
toisi d’ anestē
hērōs Atreïdēs eury kreiōn Agamemnōn
achnymenos·
sentences.i: and among them there stood up the hero Agamemnon, son of Atreus, wide-ruling, grieving;
sentences.n: The subject is held back for suspense: ἥρως ‘the hero’ (a title for a warrior of the heroic age), then the patronymic Ἀτρεΐδης ‘son of Atreus’, and only then the name. εὐρὺ κρείων is printed as two words: εὐρύ is the adverb ‘widely’ and κρείων is ‘ruling’, hence ‘wide-ruling’. τοῖσι ‘among them’ is the dative plural of the pronoun, and ἀνέστη is ‘stood up’. ἀχνύμενος, ‘grieving’, begins line 103.

sentences.t:
μένεος δὲ μέγα φρένες ἀμφιμέλαιναι
πίμπλαντ’, ὄσσε δέ οἱ πυρὶ λαμπετόωντι ἐΐκτην·
sentences.tr:
meneos de mega phrenes amphimelainai
pimplant’, osse de hoi pyri lampetoōnti eïktēn·
sentences.l:
and his heart, black all about, was greatly filled
with fury, and his two eyes were like blazing fire;
sentences.i: his heart, black through and through, swelled greatly with fury, and his eyes seemed like blazing fire;
sentences.n: Anger is shown in the body; this couplet stands word for word at Odyssey 4.661–662, with the same English. φρένες, here ‘heart’, are the seat of feeling, and ἀμφιμέλαιναι is literally ‘black all round’; the picture behind it the Greek does not say, and the translation keeps the literal word. μένεος, genitive of μένος ‘fury, force’, fills them; πίμπλαντ’ is πίμπλαντο, imperfect passive of πίμπλημι ‘fill’. ὄσσε is a dual, ‘the two eyes’, and ἐΐκτην is a dual past of ἔοικα ‘be like’, agreeing with it; the comparison is the dative πυρὶ λαμπετόωντι ‘to blazing fire’, with a stretched participle of λαμπετάω ‘blaze’. οἱ is ‘his’.

sentences.t: Κάλχαντα πρώτιστα κάκ’ ὀσσόμενος προσέειπε·
sentences.tr: Kalchanta prōtista kak’ ossomenos proseeipe·
sentences.l: Calchas first of all, evils foreboding, he addressed:
sentences.i: foreboding evil, he spoke to Calchas first of all:
sentences.n: Agamemnon turns on the seer first: Κάλχαντα is the object, put first, and πρώτιστα ‘first of all’ goes with the address. κάκ’ is κακά ‘evils’, elided. ὀσσόμενος is from ὄσσομαι, ‘foresee, forebode’, a verb probably connected with ὄσσε ‘eyes’; ‘foreboding’ is the usual sense with κακά, and the Greek does not settle whether he foresees evil in Calchas or looks it at him. προσέειπε ‘addressed’ is the epic aorist of προσεῖπον.

sentences.t: μάντι κακῶν οὐ πώ ποτέ μοι τὸ κρήγυον εἶπας·
sentences.tr: manti kakōn ou pō pote moi to krēgyon eipas·
sentences.l: “Seer of evils, never yet to me the welcome thing have you said;
sentences.i: “Seer of evils, you have never yet said anything welcome to me;
sentences.n: Agamemnon opens with an insult, and the first part of the speech is a charge against Calchas, before it turns to the prize he wants. μάντι κακῶν is a vocative: ‘seer of evils’, κακῶν being the genitive of what he is seer of. τὸ κρήγυον is ‘the welcome thing’: κρήγυος is glossed ‘good, useful’ and its origin is not known, so the translation takes the sense the line needs, and keeps ἐσθλόν (108) as ‘good’. οὐ πώ ποτε is ‘never yet’, and εἶπας is an aorist of εἶπον in the -ας form.

sentences.t:
αἰεί τοι τὰ κάκ’ ἐστὶ φίλα φρεσὶ μαντεύεσθαι,
ἐσθλὸν δ’ οὔτέ τί πω εἶπας ἔπος οὔτ’ ἐτέλεσσας·
sentences.tr:
aiei toi ta kak’ esti phila phresi manteuesthai,
esthlon d’ oute ti pō eipas epos out’ etelessas·
sentences.l:
Always for you the evils are dear to your wits to prophesy,
and a good word you have never yet spoken nor brought to pass;
sentences.i: It is always evils that your wits love to prophesy, and a good word you have never yet spoken or brought to pass;
sentences.n: τοι is σοι ‘to you’. φίλα … φρεσὶ μαντεύεσθαι is ‘dear to your wits to prophesy’: the infinitive says in what respect the evils are dear, and φίλος is ‘dear’ as always. In 108 οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’ pairs εἶπας ‘you have spoken’ with ἐτέλεσσας ‘you have brought to pass’ (τελέω, with the doubled σ the verse often asks for); ἐσθλὸν … ἔπος is ‘a good word’.

sentences.t:
καὶ νῦν ἐν Δαναοῖσι θεοπροπέων ἀγορεύεις
ὡς δὴ τοῦδ’ ἕνεκά σφιν ἑκηβόλος ἄλγεα τεύχει,
sentences.tr:
kai nyn en Danaoisi theopropeōn agoreueis
hōs dē toud’ heneka sphin hekēbolos algea teuchei,
sentences.l:
And now among the Danaans, prophesying, you declare
that indeed for the sake of this for them the far-shooter pains is making,
sentences.i: And now, prophesying among the Danaans, you declare that this is why the far-shooter is working pains for them,
sentences.n: Agamemnon now quotes Calchas’ claim against him. ἐν Δαναοῖσι ‘among the Danaans’ is a dative plural in -οισι, θεοπροπέων is the participle of θεοπροπέω ‘prophesy’, and ὡς ‘that’ opens what Calchas is said to have declared. τοῦδ’ ἕνεκα ‘for the sake of this’ points forward to οὕνεκ’ in the next line. ἑκηβόλος is Apollo, named by his epithet alone, as at 1.96; τεύχει is ‘makes, brings about’, the present of the verb that appears in the past at 1.4 (τεῦχε). ἄλγεα ‘pains’ recalls the ἄλγε’ of 1.2.

sentences.t:
οὕνεκ’ ἐγὼ κούρης Χρυσηΐδος ἀγλά’ ἄποινα
οὐκ ἔθελον δέξασθαι, ἐπεὶ πολὺ βούλομαι αὐτὴν
οἴκοι ἔχειν·
sentences.tr:
hounek’ egō kourēs Chrysēïdos agla’ apoina
ouk ethelon dexasthai, epei poly boulomai autēn
oikoi echein·
sentences.i: because I would not accept the splendid ransom for the maiden Chryseis, since I much prefer to keep her at home;
sentences.n: This is Agamemnon’s own account of 1.12–32: the girl is Chryses’ daughter, and Χρυσηΐδος (genitive of Χρυσηΐς) is a name made from her father’s, ‘Chryses’ daughter’. ἀγλά’ ἄποινα, with ἀγλά’ for ἀγλαά, is the phrase of 1.23, ‘the splendid ransom’. οὐκ ἔθελον δέξασθαι is ‘I was unwilling to accept’, i.e. I refused. πολὺ βούλομαι is ‘I much prefer’, and οἴκοι ἔχειν, ‘to keep at home’, opens the next line.

sentences.t:
καὶ γάρ ῥα Κλυταιμνήστρης προβέβουλα
κουριδίης ἀλόχου, ἐπεὶ οὔ ἑθέν ἐστι χερείων,
οὐ δέμας οὐδὲ φυήν, οὔτ’ ἂρ φρένας οὔτέ τι ἔργα.
sentences.tr:
kai gar rha Klytaimnēstrēs probeboula
kouridiēs alochou, epei ou hethen esti chereiōn,
ou demas oude phyēn, out’ ar phrenas oute ti erga.
sentences.i: for I prefer her to Clytemnestra, my wedded wife, since she is not inferior to her in body or stature, in mind or in any of her works.
sentences.n: Clytemnestra is Agamemnon’s wife, and the girl is set above her. Κλυταιμνήστρης is a genitive of comparison with προβέβουλα (perfect of προβούλομαι ‘prefer’); κουριδίης ἀλόχου ‘wedded wife’ is in apposition to it. In οὔ ἑθέν ἐστι χερείων, χερείων is the comparative ‘worse’ (Attic χείρων), and ἑθέν (= ἕθεν) is ‘than her’, meaning Clytemnestra. The four accusatives name the respects: δέμας ‘body’, φυήν ‘stature’, φρένας ‘mind’, ἔργα ‘works’, the last covering what a woman does with her hands.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς ἐθέλω δόμεναι πάλιν εἰ τό γ’ ἄμεινον·
sentences.tr: alla kai hōs ethelō domenai palin ei to g’ ameinon·
sentences.l: But even so I am willing to give back, if that at least is better;
sentences.i: Yet even so I am willing to give her back, if that is better;
sentences.n: The concession comes with a condition. ὧς is the accented form of ὡς ‘thus’, so ἀλλὰ καὶ ὧς is ‘but even so’. δόμεναι is the epic infinitive of δίδωμι (= δοῦναι), as at 1.98; ‘her’ is not expressed. εἰ τό γ’ ἄμεινον ‘if that is better’ leaves the verb ‘is’ out.

sentences.t: βούλομ’ ἐγὼ λαὸν σῶν ἔμμεναι ἢ ἀπολέσθαι·
sentences.tr: boulom’ egō laon sōn emmenai ē apolesthai·
sentences.l: I prefer the people to be safe than to perish;
sentences.i: I would rather see the people safe than perishing;
sentences.n: Agamemnon puts the army’s safety above the girl. βούλομαι … ἢ is ‘I prefer … to’ (the ἤ is ‘than’), and λαόν ‘people’ is the whole host. σῶν is the accusative of σῶς ‘safe’ (Attic σῷος), the predicate of ἔμμεναι, which is the epic infinitive of εἰμί (= εἶναι); ἀπολέσθαι is the aorist infinitive middle of ἀπόλλυμι ‘perish’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐμοὶ γέρας αὐτίχ’ ἑτοιμάσατ’ ὄφρα μὴ οἶος
Ἀργείων ἀγέραστος ἔω, ἐπεὶ οὐδὲ ἔοικε·
sentences.tr:
autar emoi geras autich’ hetoimasat’ ophra mē oios
Argeiōn agerastos eō, epei oude eoike·
sentences.l:
But for me a prize at once prepare, so that not alone
of the Argives prizeless I may be, since it is not even fitting;
sentences.i: But get a prize of honour ready for me at once, so that I alone of the Argives may not be without one, since it is not even fitting;
sentences.n: γέρας is a prize of honour, a chief’s share of the spoil that marks his rank; that is why being without one is not even ἔοικε ‘fitting’. The Argives here are the whole army. ἑτοιμάσατ’ is a plural imperative (‘prepare, all of you’), so Agamemnon is addressing the assembly, not Calchas. ἔω is the epic short-vowel subjunctive of εἰμί (Attic ὦ) after ὄφρα μή ‘so that not’, and οἶος … Ἀργείων is ‘alone of the Argives’. ἀγέραστος is ‘without a γέρας’, translated ‘prizeless’ in the literal layer.

sentences.t: λεύσσετε γὰρ τό γε πάντες ὅ μοι γέρας ἔρχεται ἄλλῃ.
sentences.tr: leussete gar to ge pantes ho moi geras erchetai allēi.
sentences.l: For you all see this, that my prize goes elsewhere.”
sentences.i: For you can all see this: my prize of honour is going elsewhere.”
sentences.n: The speech ends on its real point: the prize that is going elsewhere is his own, and Chryseis is the prize he is losing. λεύσσετε is ‘you see’, second person plural. τό γε … ὅ ‘this, that’ uses ὅ, the neuter relative, much as ὅτι ‘that’. ἄλλῃ is an adverb, ‘elsewhere, in another direction’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita podarkēs dios Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him then answered swift-footed, heavenly Achilles:
sentences.i: Then swift-footed, heavenly Achilles answered him:
sentences.n: A reply-formula, ‘Him then answered …’, the formula at 1.84 is a different one, with ἀπαμειβόμενος. ποδάρκης is an epithet of Achilles whose formation is not certain: it seems to be πούς ‘foot’ plus ἀρκέω ‘suffice, avail’, and it is understood as ‘swift-footed’. The translation keeps it apart from πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift of foot’ (1.58) and from ποδώκης. δῖος ‘heavenly’ is translated every time.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη κύδιστε φιλοκτεανώτατε πάντων,
πῶς γάρ τοι δώσουσι γέρας μεγάθυμοι Ἀχαιοί;
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē kydiste philokteanōtate pantōn,
pōs gar toi dōsousi geras megathymoi Achaioi;
sentences.l:
“Atreus’-son, most glorious, most possession-loving of all,
for how will they give you a prize, the great-hearted Achaeans?
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, most glorious, most covetous of all, how can the great-hearted Achaeans give you a prize of honour?
sentences.n: Achilles opens with two titles that cut: κύδιστε ‘most glorious’ (superlative, from κῦδος ‘glory’) and φιλοκτεανώτατε ‘most fond of possessions’ (φίλος + κτέανα ‘possessions’, superlative), with πάντων ‘of all’. Both are vocatives. γάρ makes the question a reason: no one can give him one, for there is nothing to give from. δώσουσι is a future, ‘will give’, and the stock epithet μεγάθυμοι ‘great-hearted’ goes with Ἀχαιοί.

sentences.t: οὐδέ τί που ἴδμεν ξυνήϊα κείμενα πολλά·
sentences.tr: oude ti pou idmen xynēïa keimena polla·
sentences.l: Nor do we know of any common goods lying anywhere, many;
sentences.i: And we know of no common goods lying anywhere in quantity;
sentences.n: Achilles says there is no common store to draw on. ξυνήϊα are things held in common, with the old spelling ξυν- for συν-; κείμενα ‘lying’ means lying in store, and πολλά ‘many’ goes with them. ἴδμεν is the epic first plural of οἶδα (= ἴσμεν), and οὐδέ τί που is ‘nor … any … anywhere’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τὰ μὲν πολίων ἐξεπράθομεν, τὰ δέδασται,
λαοὺς δ’ οὐκ ἐπέοικε παλίλλογα ταῦτ’ ἐπαγείρειν.
sentences.tr:
alla ta men poliōn exeprathomen, ta dedastai,
laous d’ ouk epeoike palilloga taut’ epageirein.
sentences.l:
But what from the cities we sacked-utterly, those things have been divided,
and for the people it is not fitting these things again-gathered to collect.
sentences.i: But what we took from the cities when we sacked them has been divided, and it is not fitting for the people to gather those things in again.
sentences.n: τὰ μέν … τά picks up the spoil: ‘what we plundered from the cities’ is the object of ἐξεπράθομεν, and the second τά, ‘those things’, resumes it as subject of δέδασται, the perfect passive of δατέομαι ‘divide’. ἐκπέρθω ‘sack-utterly’ is the verb of 1.19 (ἐκπέρσαι). παλίλλογα ‘gathered again’ (πάλιν + λέγω ‘gather’) is a rare word, and λαούς ‘the people’ is the subject of the infinitive ἐπαγείρειν ‘to collect’, after ἐπέοικε ‘it is fitting’ (as ἔοικε at 119).

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν νῦν τήνδε θεῷ πρόες·
sentences.tr: alla sy men nyn tēnde theōi proes·
sentences.l: But you, for now, give this one up to the god;
sentences.i: But for now, give this girl up to the god;
sentences.n: σὺ μὲν νῦν ‘you, for now’ is answered by αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοί in the next unit. πρόες is the aorist imperative of προΐημι ‘send forward, give up’, and θεῷ ‘to the god’ is Apollo, not named. τήνδε ‘this one’ is Chryseis, who is the girl in question without being named.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
τριπλῇ τετραπλῇ τ’ ἀποτείσομεν, αἴ κέ ποθι Ζεὺς
δῷσι πόλιν Τροίην εὐτείχεον ἐξαλαπάξαι.
sentences.tr:
autar Achaioi
triplēi tetraplēi t’ apoteisomen, ai ke pothi Zeus
dōisi polin Troiēn euteicheon exalapaxai.
sentences.l:
but we Achaeans
threefold and fourfold will pay back, if ever Zeus
grants us to plunder utterly the city of Troy, well-walled.”
sentences.i: but we Achaeans will repay you three times over and four, if ever Zeus grants us to plunder the well-walled city of Troy.”
sentences.n: Ἀχαιοί are Achilles’ own side, and the verb ἀποτείσομεν is first person plural, ‘we shall pay back’, future of ἀποτίνω; τριπλῇ τετραπλῇ τ’ ‘three- and four-fold’ are adverbs. αἴ κε is εἰ ἄν ‘if ever’, ποθι is που ‘ever’, and δῷσι is the aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι with the epic ending -σι (Attic δῷ); ἐξαλαπάξαι, the aorist infinitive of ἐξαλαπάζω ‘plunder utterly’, depends on it. εὐτείχεον is ‘well-walled’, with the uncontracted ending, and πόλιν Τροίην is ‘the city, Troy’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη κρείων Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē kreiōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed lord Agamemnon:
sentences.i: In answer lord Agamemnon said to him:
sentences.n: The reply-formula, as at 1.84. ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is a participle of ἀπαμείβομαι, and προσέφη ‘addressed’ is the aorist of πρόσφημι. κρείων is a participle used as a title, ‘ruling’, and the translation gives it as ‘lord’, the word the Odyssey table gives it; the line at 172 uses ἄναξ for ‘lord’ in a longer title, and the context keeps the two apart.

sentences.t:
μὴ δ’ οὕτως ἀγαθός περ ἐὼν θεοείκελ’ Ἀχιλλεῦ
κλέπτε νόῳ, ἐπεὶ οὐ παρελεύσεαι οὐδέ με πείσεις.
sentences.tr:
mē d’ houtōs agathos per eōn theoeikel’ Achilleu
klepte noōi, epei ou pareleuseai oude me peiseis.
sentences.l:
“Not thus, good though you are, god-resembling Achilles,
steal in mind, since you will not get past me nor persuade me.
sentences.i: “Do not, good as you are, Achilles, you who are like a god, try to cheat me in your mind: you will not get past me, and you will not persuade me.
sentences.n: κλέπτε νόῳ is literally ‘steal with your mind’, i.e. practise deceit; μὴ δ’ οὕτως forbids it ‘in this way’, and ἀγαθός περ ἐών is ‘good though you are’, so the compliment is made to sting. The Greek does not say what the deceit would be. θεοείκελε is the vocative of θεοείκελος ‘god-resembling’, a compliment also turned against its object. παρελεύσεαι is the future of παρέρχομαι ‘go past’, here ‘get past’ in the sense of outwit.

sentences.t:
ἦ ἐθέλεις ὄφρ’ αὐτὸς ἔχῃς γέρας, αὐτὰρ ἔμ’ αὔτως
ἧσθαι δευόμενον, κέλεαι δέ με τήνδ’ ἀποδοῦναι;
sentences.tr:
ē etheleis ophr’ autos echēis geras, autar em’ autōs
hēsthai deuomenon, keleai de me tēnd’ apodounai;
sentences.l:
Is it that you wish, so that you yourself have a prize, while me, just so,
to sit lacking, and do you bid me give back this one?
sentences.i: Is it your wish to keep a prize of honour for yourself while I just sit here lacking one, and do you tell me to give this girl back?
sentences.n: ἦ marks a question, and ἐθέλεις ὄφρ’ αὐτὸς ἔχῃς γέρας … ἔμ’ ἧσθαι is ‘you wish that you yourself have a prize … and that I sit’; the infinitive ἧσθαι is that of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and δευόμενον ‘lacking’ (a prize) agrees with ἔμ’. αὔτως is ‘just so’, i.e. as I am, with nothing. κέλεαι is the epic second person of κέλομαι ‘bid’, and ἀποδοῦναι is ‘to give back’. τήνδε ‘this one’ is Chryseis again.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰ μὲν δώσουσι γέρας μεγάθυμοι Ἀχαιοὶ
ἄρσαντες κατὰ θυμὸν ὅπως ἀντάξιον ἔσται·
sentences.tr:
all’ ei men dōsousi geras megathymoi Achaioi
arsantes kata thymon hopōs antaxion estai·
sentences.l:
But if indeed the great-hearted Achaeans will give a prize,
fitting it to my heart so that it will be of equal worth;
sentences.i: But if the great-hearted Achaeans give me a prize of honour, fitting it to my heart so that it is of equal worth —
sentences.n: The sentence has no main clause: εἰ μὲν … is left hanging, and the contrast is εἰ δέ at 137, so the reader supplies ‘well and good’. The words μεγάθυμοι Ἀχαιοί and δώσουσι γέρας repeat Achilles’ own words of 123. ἄρσαντες is the aorist participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’; κατὰ θυμόν is ‘to my heart’s liking’; ἀντάξιον is ‘of equal worth’, and ὅπως ἔσται ‘so that it shall be’ is a purpose clause with the future.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κε μὴ δώωσιν ἐγὼ δέ κεν αὐτὸς ἕλωμαι
ἢ τεὸν ἢ Αἴαντος ἰὼν γέρας, ἢ Ὀδυσῆος
ἄξω ἑλών·
sentences.tr:
ei de ke mē dōōsin egō de ken autos helōmai
ē teon ē Aiantos iōn geras, ē Odysēos
axō helōn·
sentences.i: But if they do not give, I myself will go and take your prize of honour, or Ajax’s, or Odysseus’s, and carry it off;
sentences.n: The threat is spoken to the whole assembly, and three possible victims are named: τεὸν (= σόν) ‘yours’, which agrees with γέρας, and Αἴαντος ‘of Ajax’ and Ὀδυσῆος ‘of Odysseus’, genitives that depend on it. Which Ajax is meant, the text here does not say. δώωσιν is the epic aorist subjunctive of δίδωμι; ἕλωμαι is the aorist subjunctive middle of αἱρέω ‘take’, and with κεν it is a future, ‘I shall take’. ἰών ‘going’ and ἑλών ‘having taken’ frame ἄξω ‘I will carry off’.

sentences.t: ὃ δέ κεν κεχολώσεται ὅν κεν ἵκωμαι.
sentences.tr: ho de ken kecholōsetai hon ken hikōmai.
sentences.l: and he will be angry, to whom I come.
sentences.i: and whoever I come to will be angry.
sentences.n: ὃ δέ is ‘and he’, the man whose prize it is. ὅν κεν ἵκωμαι is ‘to whom I come’: ἱκνέομαι takes the accusative, and κεν with the subjunctive makes it indefinite, ‘whoever’. κεχολώσεται is the future perfect of χολόω, from χόλος ‘anger’, ‘he will be angry’ (and stay so).

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι μὲν ταῦτα μεταφρασόμεσθα καὶ αὖτις,
νῦν δ’ ἄγε νῆα μέλαιναν ἐρύσσομεν εἰς ἅλα δῖαν,
sentences.tr:
all’ ētoi men tauta metaphrasomestha kai autis,
nyn d’ age nēa melainan eryssomen eis hala dian,
sentences.l:
But these things indeed we shall consider afterwards also,
and now come, a black ship let us drag down into the heavenly brine,
sentences.i: But we shall think about these things again later; for now, come, let us drag a black ship down into the heavenly brine,
sentences.n: Agamemnon turns from the threat to the business of sending the girl back. μεταφράζομαι is ‘consider afterwards, deliberate later’, and καὶ αὖτις is ‘also later’. νῦν δ’ ἄγε is ‘but now come’, and ἐρύσσομεν is a short-vowel subjunctive of ἐρύω ‘draw, drag’, ‘let us drag’. νῆα μέλαιναν is ‘a black ship’, and ἅλα δῖαν, with δῖος ‘heavenly’ as always, is ‘the heavenly brine’ (ἅλς is ‘salt’, hence the sea).

sentences.t:
ἐν δ’ ἐρέτας ἐπιτηδὲς ἀγείρομεν, ἐς δ’ ἑκατόμβην
θείομεν, ἂν δ’ αὐτὴν Χρυσηΐδα καλλιπάρῃον
βήσομεν·
sentences.tr:
en d’ eretas epitēdes ageiromen, es d’ hekatombēn
theiomen, an d’ autēn Chrysēïda kalliparēion
bēsomen·
sentences.i: and let us gather suitable oarsmen aboard, and place a hecatomb in her, and put Chryseis herself, fair-cheeked, on board;
sentences.n: Three verbs, each with its preverb parted from it (tmesis): ἐν … ἀγείρομεν ‘gather in’, ἐς … θείομεν ‘place in’, ἂν … βήσομεν ‘make go up’ (ἂν is ἀνά). All are hortative subjunctives with a short vowel (θείομεν is the epic form for θῶμεν). ἐπιτηδές is ‘for the purpose, as needed’; ἑκατόμβη is a great sacrifice (the ‘hecatomb’ of 1.65). καλλιπάρῃον is ‘fair-cheeked’, from παρῃά ‘cheek’.

sentences.t:
εἷς δέ τις ἀρχὸς ἀνὴρ βουληφόρος ἔστω,
ἢ Αἴας ἢ Ἰδομενεὺς ἢ δῖος Ὀδυσσεὺς
ἠὲ σὺ Πηλεΐδη πάντων ἐκπαγλότατ’ ἀνδρῶν,
ὄφρ’ ἥμιν ἑκάεργον ἱλάσσεαι ἱερὰ ῥέξας.
sentences.tr:
heis de tis archos anēr boulēphoros estō,
ē Aias ē Idomeneus ē dios Odysseus
ēe sy Pēleïdē pantōn ekpaglotat’ andrōn,
ophr’ hēmin hekaergon hilasseai hiera rhexas.
sentences.l:
and let one man be leader, a man of counsel,
either Ajax or Idomeneus or heavenly Odysseus,
or you, son of Peleus, most terrifying of all men,
that for us the far-working one you may propitiate, having performed the sacrifices.”
sentences.i: and let one man of counsel be its leader — Ajax, or Idomeneus, or heavenly Odysseus, or you, son of Peleus, most terrifying of all men — so that you may appease for us the one who works from afar by performing the sacrifices.”
sentences.n: The list of possible leaders ends with Achilles himself, whom Agamemnon calls ἐκπαγλότατ’ ἀνδρῶν ‘most terrifying of men’; ἔκπαγλος ‘striking, terrifying’ is a strong word, and here it may be taken as praise or as a jab. βουληφόρος is ‘counsel-bearing’, a man of counsel; ἔστω is a third-person imperative. Πηλεΐδη is a vocative patronymic, ‘son of Peleus’. ἑκάεργον is an epithet of Apollo, translated ‘far-working’ and glossed ‘who works from afar’; its sense is disputed, and it is a different word from ἑκηβόλος. ἱλάσσεαι is the subjunctive of ἱλάσκομαι ‘propitiate, appease’, and ἱερὰ ῥέξας ‘having performed the sacrifices’ says how.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Then Achilles, swift of foot, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: The scowl-formula: ὑπόδρα ἰδών ‘looking at him with a scowl’. The ancient explanation of ὑπόδρα is ‘from under the brows’, and the derivation is not certain. πόδας ὠκύς is ‘swift of foot’, with the accusative πόδας ‘in respect of the feet’, and προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘addressed’.

sentences.l:
“Ah me, in shamelessness clothed, gain-minded one,
how shall any of the Achaeans readily obey your words
either to go a journey or with men with force to fight?
sentences.i: “Ah me, you clothed in shamelessness, with your mind on gain, how can any Achaean readily obey your words, whether to go on a journey or to fight men powerfully?
sentences.n: ὤ μοι is an exclamation of dismay (‘ah me’), followed by two vocatives. ἀναιδείην ἐπιειμένε is ‘you who are clothed in shamelessness’, the perfect middle participle of ἐπιέννυμι with the accusative of what is worn. κερδαλεόφρον is κέρδος ‘gain’ plus φρήν ‘mind’, ‘gain-minded’, answering φιλοκτεανώτατε of 122. In the question, πείθηται is a deliberative subjunctive (‘how is anyone to obey’) with the dative ἔπεσιν ‘your words’, Ἀχαιῶν is partitive, and ὁδὸν ἐλθέμεναι is ‘to go on a journey’, with the epic infinitive in -έμεναι. ἶφι is ‘with force’.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐγὼ Τρώων ἕνεκ’ ἤλυθον αἰχμητάων
δεῦρο μαχησόμενος, ἐπεὶ οὔ τί μοι αἴτιοί εἰσιν·
sentences.tr:
ou gar egō Trōōn henek’ ēlython aichmētaōn
deuro machēsomenos, epei ou ti moi aitioi eisin·
sentences.l:
For not I because of the Trojans, spearmen, came
here to fight, since not at all to me are they to blame;
sentences.i: For I did not come here to fight because of the Trojan spearmen, since they are not at all to blame towards me;
sentences.n: Achilles’ first grievance is that he has no quarrel with Troy. Τρώων … αἰχμητάων is ‘the spearman Trojans’, αἰχμητής being ‘spearman’, and ἕνεκ’ ‘on account of’ follows the genitive. μαχησόμενος is a future participle of purpose, ‘to fight’. αἴτιοι is ‘to blame’, and μοι ‘to me’ says toward whom.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ πώποτ’ ἐμὰς βοῦς ἤλασαν οὐδὲ μὲν ἵππους,
οὐδέ ποτ’ ἐν Φθίῃ ἐριβώλακι βωτιανείρῃ
καρπὸν ἐδηλήσαντ’, ἐπεὶ ἦ μάλα πολλὰ μεταξὺ
οὔρεά τε σκιόεντα θάλασσά τε ἠχήεσσα·
sentences.tr:
ou gar pōpot’ emas bous ēlasan oude men hippous,
oude pot’ en Phthiēi eribōlaki bōtianeirēi
karpon edēlēsant’, epei ē mala polla metaxy
ourea te skioenta thalassa te ēchēessa·
sentences.i: for they never drove off my cattle or my horses, nor ever harmed the crop in Phthia, rich-soiled nurse of men, since truly a great deal lies between us: the shadowy mountains and the resounding sea;
sentences.n: Phthia is Achilles’ homeland, and the long reason is that it is too far away for the Trojans to have wronged him. ἐριβώλακι is ‘rich-soiled’, and βωτιανείρῃ is ‘man-nourishing’, with a first element from the root of βόσκω ‘feed’; both are datives agreeing with Φθίῃ. ἤλασαν is the aorist of ἐλαύνω ‘drive off’, ἐδηλήσαντ’ the aorist middle of δηλέομαι ‘harm’, and βοῦς is feminine plural, ‘cattle’. In 156 ἦ μάλα πολλὰ μεταξύ is ‘in truth very many things between’, with ‘lie’ understood; οὔρεα is the Ionic plural of ὄρος, and ἠχήεσσα is ‘resounding’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ σοὶ ὦ μέγ’ ἀναιδὲς ἅμ’ ἑσπόμεθ’ ὄφρα σὺ χαίρῃς,
τιμὴν ἀρνύμενοι Μενελάῳ σοί τε κυνῶπα
πρὸς Τρώων·
sentences.tr:
alla soi ō meg’ anaides ham’ hespometh’ ophra sy chairēis,
timēn arnymenoi Menelaōi soi te kynōpa
pros Trōōn·
sentences.i: But we followed you along, utterly shameless man, so that you might rejoice, winning honour from the Trojans for Menelaus and for you, you dog-face;
sentences.n: κυνῶπα is a vocative, ‘dog-face’: κύων ‘dog’ plus ὤψ ‘face, eye’. The dog stands for shamelessness, so it overlaps μέγ’ ἀναιδές ‘utterly shameless’; the feminine κυνῶπις is Helen’s name for herself in the Odyssey. ἑσπόμεθ’ is the aorist of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ with the dative σοί, and ἅμ’ is ‘along’. τιμὴν ἀρνύμενοι is ‘winning honour’; τιμή here has the sense of satisfaction owed for a wrong, and πρὸς Τρώων is ‘from the Trojans’.

sentences.t: τῶν οὔ τι μετατρέπῃ οὐδ’ ἀλεγίζεις·
sentences.tr: tōn ou ti metatrepēi oud’ alegizeis·
sentences.l: to none of which you pay regard, nor do you care;
sentences.i: and you pay no regard to any of it, nor do you care;
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of which’ is plural and takes in the whole business of winning honour from the Trojans. μετατρέπῃ is a second-person middle, ‘you turn to, pay regard to’, with a genitive, and ἀλεγίζεις is ‘you care for’; οὔ τι … οὐδέ is ‘not at all … nor’.

sentences.t:
καὶ δή μοι γέρας αὐτὸς ἀφαιρήσεσθαι ἀπειλεῖς,
ᾧ ἔπι πολλὰ μόγησα, δόσαν δέ μοι υἷες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
kai dē moi geras autos aphairēsesthai apeileis,
hōi epi polla mogēsa, dosan de moi huies Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
And now my prize you yourself threaten to take away,
for which I toiled much, and gave it to me the sons of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: And now you yourself threaten to take away my prize of honour, the one I toiled so hard for and the sons of the Achaeans gave me.
sentences.n: αὐτός ‘you yourself’ says that it is Agamemnon, not the army, who is taking it. ἀφαιρήσεσθαι is a future middle infinitive after ἀπειλεῖς ‘you threaten’. ᾧ ἔπι is ἐπὶ ᾧ, the preposition after its word, ‘for which’; μόγησα is the aorist of μογέω ‘toil’, and δόσαν is ἔδοσαν without the augment. υἷες Ἀχαιῶν ‘sons of the Achaeans’ is a poetic way of saying the Achaeans.

sentences.t:
οὐ μὲν σοί ποτε ἶσον ἔχω γέρας ὁππότ’ Ἀχαιοὶ
Τρώων ἐκπέρσωσ’ εὖ ναιόμενον πτολίεθρον·
sentences.tr:
ou men soi pote ison echō geras hoppot’ Achaioi
Trōōn ekpersōs’ eu naiomenon ptoliethron·
sentences.l:
Never do I have a prize equal to yours, whenever the Achaeans
sack-utterly of the Trojans a well-inhabited citadel;
sentences.i: Never do I have a prize of honour equal to yours, whenever the Achaeans sack a well-inhabited citadel of the Trojans;
sentences.n: Here Achilles complains about the shares. σοί ποτε ἶσον is ‘equal to yours’ (σοί is a dative of comparison), and ὁππότε with the aorist subjunctive ἐκπέρσωσ’ (= ἐκπέρσωσι) is ‘whenever they sack’. Τρώων is possessive with πτολίεθρον, an epic extension of πόλις, ‘a citadel of the Trojans’, and εὖ ναιόμενον is ‘well-inhabited’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν πλεῖον πολυάϊκος πολέμοιο
χεῖρες ἐμαὶ διέπουσ’·
sentences.tr:
alla to men pleion polyaïkos polemoio
cheires emai diepous’·
sentences.l:
but the greater part of the much-rushing war
my hands carry through;
sentences.i: but it is my hands that carry through the greater part of the onrushing war;
sentences.n: The meaning of πολυάϊκος is not certain: it appears to belong with ἀΐσσω ‘rush’, and the translation takes it as ‘much-rushing’, of the war. τὸ πλεῖον is ‘the greater part’, the object of διέπουσ’ (= διέπουσι), ‘carry through, manage’, and χεῖρες ἐμαί is ‘my hands’. The μέν clause is answered by ἀτάρ in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἤν ποτε δασμὸς ἵκηται,
σοὶ τὸ γέρας πολὺ μεῖζον, ἐγὼ δ’ ὀλίγον τε φίλον τε
ἔρχομ’ ἔχων ἐπὶ νῆας, ἐπεί κε κάμω πολεμίζων.
sentences.tr:
atar ēn pote dasmos hikētai,
soi to geras poly meizon, egō d’ oligon te philon te
erchom’ echōn epi nēas, epei ke kamō polemizōn.
sentences.l:
but if ever the division comes,
to you the prize is much greater, and I, a small thing and a dear one,
go with it to the ships, when I have grown weary fighting.
sentences.i: but if ever the sharing-out comes, the far bigger prize of honour is yours, while I go back to the ships with something small though dear to me, when I have worn myself out fighting.
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ ἤν ποτε is ‘but if ever’ (ἤν = ἐάν), and δασμός is the division of the spoil; ἵκηται is a subjunctive. σοὶ τὸ γέρας πολὺ μεῖζον has no verb, ‘to you the much greater prize’. ὀλίγον τε φίλον τε is ‘small and dear’, φίλον being ‘dear’ as always. ἔρχομ’ ἔχων is ‘I go with it’, and ἐπεί κε κάμω is ‘when I have grown weary’, aorist subjunctive of κάμνω with κε.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ εἶμι Φθίην δ’, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτερόν ἐστιν
οἴκαδ’ ἴμεν σὺν νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν, οὐδέ σ’ ὀΐω
ἐνθάδ’ ἄτιμος ἐὼν ἄφενος καὶ πλοῦτον ἀφύξειν.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ eimi Phthiēn d’, epei ē poly pherteron estin
oikad’ imen syn nēusi korōnisin, oude s’ oïō
enthad’ atimos eōn aphenos kai plouton aphyxein.
sentences.l:
But now I am going to Phthia, since truly it is much better
to go home with curved ships, and I do not think, for you,
here being dishonoured, wealth and riches to draw up.”
sentences.i: But now I am going to Phthia, since it is truly much better to go home in curved ships — and I do not think that here, dishonoured, I shall go on piling up wealth and riches for you.”
sentences.n: Achilles threatens to leave. Φθίην δ’ is Φθίηνδε ‘to Phthia’, the suffix -δε of direction, printed as a separate elided word; εἶμι is ‘I am going’. ἴμεν is the epic infinitive of εἶμι. νηυσὶ κορωνίσιν is ‘curved ships’. In οὐδέ σ’ ὀΐω, σ’ is read as an elided σοί ‘for you’, and the nominative ἄτιμος ἐών ‘being dishonoured’ shows that Achilles himself is the subject of ἀφύξειν, the future infinitive of ἀφύσσω ‘draw up’, literally of drawing liquid. ἄφενος and πλοῦτος are both ‘wealth’; the translation gives ‘wealth and riches’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: Him then answered the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: Then Agamemnon, lord of men, answered him:
sentences.n: The same reply-formula as 1.121, with ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ in place of Achilles’ epithets; the title is the one of 1.7. ἠμείβετο ‘answered’ and ἔπειτα ‘then’ are as before.

sentences.t:
φεῦγε μάλ’ εἴ τοι θυμὸς ἐπέσσυται, οὐδέ σ’ ἔγωγε
λίσσομαι εἵνεκ’ ἐμεῖο μένειν·
sentences.tr:
pheuge mal’ ei toi thymos epessytai, oude s’ egōge
lissomai heinek’ emeio menein·
sentences.l:
“Flee, by all means, if your heart is driven to it; nor do I, for my part,
beg you to stay for my sake;
sentences.i: “Flee, then, by all means, if your heart is set on it; I for one shall not beg you to stay on my account;
sentences.n: φεῦγε is ‘flee’, a word for running away, thrown back at Achilles’ εἶμι Φθίην δ’. ἐπέσσυται is the perfect passive of ἐπισεύω ‘drive on’, so ‘if your heart has been driven to it’, and τοι is σοι. οὐδέ σ’ ἔγωγε is ‘nor I, for my part, you’, and εἵνεκ’ ἐμεῖο μένειν is ‘to stay for my sake’ (εἵνεκα is ἕνεκα, ἐμεῖο the epic genitive of ἐγώ).

sentences.t:
πάρ’ ἔμοιγε καὶ ἄλλοι
οἵ κέ με τιμήσουσι, μάλιστα δὲ μητίετα Ζεύς.
sentences.tr:
par’ emoige kai alloi
hoi ke me timēsousi, malista de mētieta Zeus.
sentences.l:
beside me there are others also
who will honour me, and most of all counsellor Zeus.
sentences.i: I have others with me who will honour me, and above all Zeus the counsellor.
sentences.n: πάρ’ ἔμοιγε is παρ’ ἔμοιγε ‘beside me’, with ‘there are’ understood; οἵ κέ με τιμήσουσι is ‘who will honour me’, the relative with κε and the future. μητίετα, from μῆτις ‘counsel’, is a stock epithet of Zeus, translated ‘counsellor’ every time, even where the counsel is harmful.

sentences.t: ἔχθιστος δέ μοί ἐσσι διοτρεφέων βασιλήων·
sentences.tr: echthistos de moi essi diotrepheōn basilēōn·
sentences.l: And most hateful to me are you of the Zeus-nurtured kings;
sentences.i: To me you are the most hateful of the Zeus-nurtured kings;
sentences.n: ἔχθιστος is the superlative of ἐχθρός ‘hateful’, and διοτρεφέων βασιλήων is a partitive genitive plural, ‘of the Zeus-nurtured kings’, with the uncontracted ending -έων on the adjective and the Homeric -ήων on the noun. διοτρεφής is a courtesy title of kings, and here it is used while Agamemnon denies Achilles the respect that goes with it.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ γάρ τοι ἔρις τε φίλη πόλεμοί τε μάχαι τε·
sentences.tr: aiei gar toi eris te philē polemoi te machai te·
sentences.l: for always strife is dear to you, and wars and battles;
sentences.i: for strife is always dear to you, and wars and battles;
sentences.n: γάρ gives the reason for the hatred. φίλη is singular and agrees with ἔρις alone, the nearest noun, though it serves all three: ‘strife is dear to you, and wars and battles’. τοι is σοι.

sentences.t: εἰ μάλα καρτερός ἐσσι, θεός που σοὶ τό γ’ ἔδωκεν·
sentences.tr: ei mala karteros essi, theos pou soi to g’ edōken·
sentences.l: if you are very strong, a god, I suppose, gave you that;
sentences.i: If you are so very strong, it was a god, I suppose, who gave you that;
sentences.n: The sneer is that strength is a gift and no ground for honour. ἐσσι is the epic second person of εἰμί, που ‘I suppose’ softens the claim, and τό γε ‘that’ is Achilles’ strength.

sentences.t:
οἴκαδ’ ἰὼν σὺν νηυσί τε σῇς καὶ σοῖς ἑτάροισι
Μυρμιδόνεσσιν ἄνασσε, σέθεν δ’ ἐγὼ οὐκ ἀλεγίζω,
οὐδ’ ὄθομαι κοτέοντος·
sentences.tr:
oikad’ iōn syn nēusi te sēis kai sois hetaroisi
Myrmidonessin anasse, sethen d’ egō ouk alegizō,
oud’ othomai koteontos·
sentences.i: Go home with your ships and your companions and be lord over the Myrmidons; I do not care about you, and I take no heed of your resentment;
sentences.n: οἴκαδ’ is οἴκαδε ‘homeward’ (-δε of direction). Μυρμιδόνεσσιν ἄνασσε is ‘be lord over the Myrmidons’, ἀνάσσω taking the dative; the Myrmidons are Achilles’ own men, whom Agamemnon sends him home to rule. σέθεν is the epic genitive of σύ, with ἀλεγίζω ‘care for’. ὄθομαι ‘heed’ is a verb found mostly in negative sentences, and κοτέοντος is the genitive participle of κοτέω ‘bear a grudge’, agreeing with an unstated ‘your’.

sentences.t: ἀπειλήσω δέ τοι ὧδε·
sentences.tr: apeilēsō de toi hōde·
sentences.l: and I will threaten you thus:
sentences.i: and this is how I will threaten you:
sentences.n: ἀπειλήσω ‘I will threaten’ answers Achilles’ ἀπειλεῖς at 161; ὧδε ‘thus’ points to what follows, and τοι is σοι. What he threatens comes in the next two units.

sentences.t:
ὡς ἔμ’ ἀφαιρεῖται Χρυσηΐδα Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων,
τὴν μὲν ἐγὼ σὺν νηΐ τ’ ἐμῇ καὶ ἐμοῖς ἑτάροισι
πέμψω,
sentences.tr:
hōs em’ aphaireitai Chrysēïda Phoibos Apollōn,
tēn men egō syn nēï t’ emēi kai emois hetaroisi
pempsō,
sentences.l:
Since Phoebus Apollo is taking Chryseis from me,
her I with my ship and with my companions
will send,
sentences.i: Since Phoebus Apollo is taking Chryseis from me, I shall send her with my ship and my companions,
sentences.n: ὡς here is ‘since’, and the τὴν μέν ‘her, on the one hand’ is answered by ἐγὼ δέ in the next unit. ἀφαιρεῖται takes two accusatives, ἔμ’ ‘me’ and Χρυσηΐδα, ‘takes Chryseis away from me’. Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is the god’s full name, and νηΐ is the dative of ναῦς ‘ship’.

sentences.t:
ἐγὼ δέ κ’ ἄγω Βρισηΐδα καλλιπάρῃον
αὐτὸς ἰὼν κλισίην δὲ τὸ σὸν γέρας ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῇς
ὅσσον φέρτερός εἰμι σέθεν, στυγέῃ δὲ καὶ ἄλλος
ἶσον ἐμοὶ φάσθαι καὶ ὁμοιωθήμεναι ἄντην.
sentences.tr:
egō de k’ agō Brisēïda kalliparēion
autos iōn klisiēn de to son geras ophr’ eÿ eidēis
hosson pherteros eimi sethen, stygeēi de kai allos
ison emoi phasthai kai homoiōthēmenai antēn.
sentences.l:
but I will lead off Briseis, fair-cheeked,
myself going to the hut — your prize — that you may know well
how much stronger I am than you, and another may loathe
to call himself equal to me and to liken himself face to face.”
sentences.i: but I myself will go to the hut and lead away Briseis, fair-cheeked, your prize of honour, so that you may know well how much stronger I am than you, and so that anyone else may hate to call himself my equal and to match himself with me to my face.”
sentences.n: Βρισηΐδα is Briseis, named here for the first time. κ’ ἄγω is κε ἄγω, a short-vowel subjunctive with κε, ‘I shall lead off’; κλισίην δέ is κλισίηνδε ‘to the hut’ (-δε of direction), and τὸ σὸν γέρας ‘your prize’ is in apposition to Βρισηΐδα. ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῇς is ‘so that you may know well’. σέθεν after φέρτερος ‘stronger’ is a genitive of comparison, στυγέῃ is the subjunctive of στυγέω ‘shrink from, hate’, φάσθαι is the infinitive of φημί ‘to say’, ὁμοιωθήμεναι is the aorist passive infinitive ‘to be made like, to compare oneself’, and ἄντην is ‘face to face’.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο·
sentences.tr: hōs phato·
sentences.l: So he spoke;
sentences.i: So he spoke;
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is the formula that closes a speech; φάτο ‘spoke’ has no augment. Here it closes Agamemnon’s speech, and the sentence goes on in the next unit with Achilles’ reaction.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐωνι δ’ ἄχος γένετ’, ἐν δέ οἱ ἦτορ
στήθεσσιν λασίοισι διάνδιχα μερμήριξεν,
sentences.tr:
Pēleïōni d’ achos genet’, en de hoi ētor
stēthessin lasioisi diandicha mermērixen,
sentences.l:
and grief came to the son of Peleus, and within him the heart
in his shaggy chest in two ways was in doubt,
sentences.i: and grief came to the son of Peleus; and the heart in his shaggy chest was in doubt between two courses,
sentences.n: Πηλεΐωνι is ‘to the son of Peleus’, a patronymic standing for Achilles, and ἄχος is ‘grief’; γένετ’ is ἐγένετο without the augment. ἐν δέ οἱ ἦτορ στήθεσσιν λασίοισι is ‘and within him the heart in his shaggy chest’, with the dative plural in -εσσιν and λάσιος ‘shaggy, hairy’. μερμήριξεν is the aorist of μερμηρίζω ‘be in doubt’ and διάνδιχα is ‘in two ways’; the two ways are given in 190–192.

sentences.t:
ἢ ὅ γε φάσγανον ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ
τοὺς μὲν ἀναστήσειεν, ὃ δ’ Ἀτρεΐδην ἐναρίζοι,
ἦε χόλον παύσειεν ἐρητύσειέ τε θυμόν.
sentences.tr:
ē ho ge phasganon oxy eryssamenos para mērou
tous men anastēseien, ho d’ Atreïdēn enarizoi,
ēe cholon pauseien erētyseie te thymon.
sentences.l:
whether, drawing his sharp sword from beside his thigh,
he should make those stand up, and himself kill the son of Atreus,
or stop his anger and restrain his heart.
sentences.i: whether he should draw the sharp sword from beside his thigh, make the others stand up, and himself kill the son of Atreus, or stop his anger and restrain his heart.
sentences.n: The two courses are an indirect question, ἢ … ἦε ‘whether … or’, with optatives (ἀναστήσειεν, ἐναρίζοι, παύσειεν, ἐρητύσειε) as in ‘wondering whether he should’. ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρύω ‘draw’, and παρὰ μηροῦ is ‘from beside the thigh’. τοὺς μὲν ἀναστήσειεν is ‘make those stand up’; the Greek does not say why. ὃ δ’ Ἀτρεΐδην ἐναρίζοι is ‘and he kill the son of Atreus’, and the second course is χόλον παύσειεν ‘stop his anger’ and ἐρητύσειέ τε θυμόν ‘restrain his heart’.

sentences.t:
ἧος ὃ ταῦθ’ ὥρμαινε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
ἕλκετο δ’ ἐκ κολεοῖο μέγα ξίφος, ἦλθε δ’ Ἀθήνη
οὐρανόθεν·
sentences.tr:
hēos ho tauth’ hōrmaine kata phrena kai kata thymon,
helketo d’ ek koleoio mega xiphos, ēlthe d’ Athēnē
ouranothen·
sentences.i: While he was turning this over in his mind and heart, and was drawing the great sword from its sheath, Athena came from the sky;
sentences.n: Two imperfects that are still unfinished, ὥρμαινε ‘was pondering’ and ἕλκετο ‘was drawing’, are cut across by the aorist ἦλθε ‘came’. ἧος is ‘while’, κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν is ‘in mind and in heart’, and ἐκ κολεοῖο is ‘from the sheath’ (genitive in -οιο). οὐρανόθεν ‘from heaven’ begins line 195.

sentences.t:
πρὸ γὰρ ἧκε θεὰ λευκώλενος Ἥρη
ἄμφω ὁμῶς θυμῷ φιλέουσά τε κηδομένη τε·
sentences.tr:
pro gar hēke thea leukōlenos Hērē
amphō homōs thymōi phileousa te kēdomenē te·
sentences.l:
for forth sent her the goddess, white-armed Hera,
both alike in heart loving and caring for;
sentences.i: for the goddess, white-armed Hera, had sent her forth, loving and caring for them both alike in her heart;
sentences.n: This says why Athena came. πρὸ … ἧκε is a tmesis, ‘sent forth’ (aorist of ἵημι), with Athena understood as the object. ἄμφω ὁμῶς is ‘both alike’, Achilles and Agamemnon, and the participles φιλέουσα (uncontracted) ‘loving’ and κηδομένη ‘caring for’ describe Hera. λευκώλενος is ‘white-armed’, translated every time.

sentences.t:
στῆ δ’ ὄπιθεν, ξανθῆς δὲ κόμης ἕλε Πηλεΐωνα
οἴῳ φαινομένη·
sentences.tr:
stē d’ opithen, xanthēs de komēs hele Pēleïōna
oiōi phainomenē·
sentences.l:
She stood behind, and by the fair hair took the son of Peleus,
appearing to him alone;
sentences.i: She stood behind him and took the son of Peleus by his fair hair, appearing to him alone;
sentences.n: στῆ is ἔστη without the augment, and ὄπιθεν is ‘behind’. ξανθῆς κόμης is a genitive of the part that is taken hold of, ‘by the fair hair’, with ἕλε ‘took’. Πηλεΐωνα is ‘the son of Peleus’, Achilles, and οἴῳ φαινομένη is ‘appearing to him alone’, with οἴῳ ‘alone’ in the dative and φαινομένη the feminine participle of φαίνομαι.

sentences.t: τῶν δ’ ἄλλων οὔ τις ὁρᾶτο·
sentences.tr: tōn d’ allōn ou tis horato·
sentences.l: of the others no one saw;
sentences.i: none of the others saw her;
sentences.n: τῶν δ’ ἄλλων is ‘of the others’, a partitive genitive with οὔ τις. ὁρᾶτο is an imperfect of ὁράω with a middle ending, ‘was seeing’, and the one seen, Athena, is understood. Athena is visible to Achilles only.

sentences.t:
θάμβησεν δ’ Ἀχιλεύς, μετὰ δ’ ἐτράπετ’, αὐτίκα δ’ ἔγνω
Παλλάδ’ Ἀθηναίην·
sentences.tr:
thambēsen d’ Achileus, meta d’ etrapet’, autika d’ egnō
Pallad’ Athēnaiēn·
sentences.l:
and Achilles was struck with wonder, and turned about, and at once knew
Pallas Athena;
sentences.i: Achilles was struck with wonder, and turned round, and at once knew her for Pallas Athena;
sentences.n: Three quick aorists: θάμβησεν ‘was struck with wonder’ (from θάμβος ‘wonder’), μετὰ … ἐτράπετ’ ‘turned about’ (a tmesis, ἐτράπετ’ for ἐτράπετο), and ἔγνω ‘recognised’. Ἀχιλεύς is spelled with a single λ here, as Ἀχιλῆος was in 1.1, for the metre. Παλλάδ’ Ἀθηναίην is ‘Pallas Athena’, with the accusative Ἀθηναίην of the form Ἀθηναίη (= Ἀθήνη).

sentences.t: δεινὼ δέ οἱ ὄσσε φάανθεν·
sentences.tr: deinō de hoi osse phaanthen·
sentences.l: and dread her two eyes shone;
sentences.i: and her eyes shone dread;
sentences.n: δεινὼ … ὄσσε is a dual, ‘the two eyes’, and δεινός is ‘dread’, as always. φάανθεν is an aorist passive of φαίνω, ‘shone, appeared’, in the plural although the subject is dual. οἱ is read as ‘her’, a dative of possession pointing to Athena, as at 104 it pointed to Agamemnon’s eyes; it could also be heard as ‘to him’.

sentences.t: καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and, lifting his voice, to her winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to her:
sentences.n: The same line stands in the Odyssey, and the English is the same. μιν is the epic accusative ‘her’ (Athena); φωνήσας is ‘lifting his voice’; ἔπεα πτερόεντα ‘winged words’ is the formula usually explained as words that fly from speaker to hearer; and προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’.

sentences.t: τίπτ’ αὖτ’ αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος εἰλήλουθας;
sentences.tr: tipt’ aut’ aigiochoio Dios tekos eilēlouthas;
sentences.l: “Why again, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, have you come?
sentences.i: “Why have you come now, child of aegis-bearing Zeus?
sentences.n: τίπτ’ is τί ποτε ‘why ever’. αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘again’; in a question like this it is closer to ‘now’, and the text does not say that Athena had come before. Διὸς τέκος is a vocative, ‘child of Zeus’ (τέκος is neuter), and αἰγιόχοιο ‘aegis-bearing’ is the traditional rendering of a word whose formation is disputed. εἰλήλουθας is the perfect of ἔρχομαι ‘you have come’, with the epic reduplication (Attic ἐλήλυθας).

sentences.t: ἦ ἵνα ὕβριν ἴδῃ Ἀγαμέμνονος Ἀτρεΐδαο;
sentences.tr: ē hina hybrin idēi Agamemnonos Atreïdao;
sentences.l: Is it that you may see the insolence of Agamemnon, Atreus’ son?
sentences.i: Is it so that you may see the insolence of Agamemnon, son of Atreus?
sentences.n: ἦ marks the question, and ἵνα with the subjunctive ἴδῃ ‘so that you may see’ gives the scornful purpose. ὕβρις is violent, contemptuous behaviour, ‘insolence’, and Ἀτρεΐδαο is the epic genitive in -αο.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἔκ τοι ἐρέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τελέεσθαι ὀΐω·
sentences.tr: all’ ek toi ereō, to de kai teleesthai oïō·
sentences.l: But I will speak out plainly to you, and this too, I think, will be fulfilled:
sentences.i: But I will tell you plainly, and I think it will come true as well:
sentences.n: ἔκ τοι ἐρέω is a tmesis, ἐξερέω ‘I will speak out, say plainly’, with τοι = σοι. τὸ δὲ καὶ τελέεσθαι ὀΐω is ‘and this too, I think, will be fulfilled’, τελέεσθαι being the uncontracted future infinitive of τελέω; ὀΐω is ‘I think’.

sentences.t: ᾗς ὑπεροπλίῃσι τάχ’ ἄν ποτε θυμὸν ὀλέσσῃ.
sentences.tr: hēis hyperopliēisi tach’ an pote thymon olessēi.
sentences.l: by his own acts of arrogance soon perhaps he may lose his life.”
sentences.i: Through his own arrogance he may perhaps soon lose his life.”
sentences.n: The speech ends with a prophecy about Agamemnon, who is not named. ᾗς is the possessive ‘his own’, agreeing with ὑπεροπλίῃσι, the dative plural of ὑπεροπλίη ‘overweening acts’. τάχ’ ἄν ποτε is ‘soon, perhaps’, and ὀλέσσῃ is the aorist subjunctive of ὄλλυμι with ἄν, ‘he may lose’. θυμόν here is the life that leaves the body, so ‘life’ and not ‘heart’.
